summary: Summarizes current practices, problems, and solutions for multipath routing, where a router has several next hops for a destination and must pick one for each packet.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router has several equal-cost paths, it should keep packets from the same flow on one path. RFC 2991 compares methods that balance traffic while limiting packet reordering and path changes.

questions: why is round robin bad for multipath routing

subtitle: How routers can choose next hops without splitting a flow across changing paths.

tldr.problem: A router with several equal-cost next hops must choose one for each packet, but round-robin or random choices can reorder packets and vary path MTU.
tldr.mechanism: Keep each flow on one path by hashing fields that identify the flow. The memo compares modulo-N hashing, hash-threshold, and Highest Random Weight (HRW).
tldr.outcome: The memo recommends HRW when per-flow state is available and for multicast; without per-flow state, it recommends hash-threshold when CPU cost matters.

facts.label: Fast-retransmit trigger
facts.value: 3 or more later packets arrive first

today: RFC 2991 is an Informational memo from November 2000, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its companion analysis of hash-threshold is RFC 2992.

sections.title: Problems with Per-Packet Path Choices
sections.content:
Equal-Cost Multipath routing gives a forwarder several next hops for one destination. If it chooses a different path for each packet, different path MTUs can defeat path MTU discovery and different delays can reorder packets.

Reordering can cause TCP to treat a delayed packet as lost; the RFC says three or more later packets arriving first can trigger fast retransmit. Tools such as ping and traceroute can also give less reliable results when traffic takes multiple paths. Multicast routing needs one next hop toward the tree root to avoid loops and duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets from one flow can arrive out of order if they take paths with different delays. Keeping that flow on one path also makes path MTU discovery and network diagnosis more reliable.

sections.title: Requirements for Next-Hop Selection
sections.content:
The memo uses flow to mean the traffic group for which a router may keep state. Depending on the implementation, a flow can be identified by a destination address or by source address, destination address, and protocol ID. The memo cautions that transport-layer fields may be absent from fragments.

A useful method keeps packets in one flow on the same path, changes as few active flows as possible when a next hop is added or removed, and uses little computation per packet.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is the set of packets that the router keeps together for path selection. A good method keeps that flow on one path and limits how many flows move when routes change.

sections.title: Three Next-Hop Selection Methods
sections.content:
Modulo-N hashing uses flow fields and takes the result modulo the number of next hops. It is fast, but adding or removing a next hop changes the path for (N-1)/N of flows. Hash-threshold assigns each next hop a region of hash values; the memo says between 1/4 and 1/2 of flows change when a next hop is added or removed.

Highest Random Weight (HRW) hashes the flow fields with each next-hop address and chooses the highest result. It affects 1/N of flows when a next hop changes, but costs about N times as much as modulo-N hashing.
sections.plainLanguage: Modulo-N is fast but can move most flows when the next-hop list changes. Hash-threshold and HRW move fewer flows, while HRW requires more calculation.

sections.title: Recommendations for Unicast and Multicast
sections.content:
When a forwarder keeps per-flow state, it can compute the next hop when the state is created. The memo recommends HRW for stable path selection. For unicast without per-flow state, it recommends hash-threshold when CPU use matters more than path stability.

Multicast forwarders keep per-flow state, so the memo recommends HRW for multicast. For PIM-SM, it also recommends using multipath information when selecting a neighbor for a join. Hash-based methods distribute flows evenly when their hash is uniform, which the memo says suits routers carrying many flows.
sections.plainLanguage: Use HRW when a router keeps per-flow state, including for multicast. Without that state, hash-threshold is the recommended option when calculation cost matters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says the next-hop selection methods do not directly affect the security of Internet infrastructure or applications. It notes that predictable selection can let an attacker create traffic that hashes onto one path and overloads it.

Multipath and less predictable hashing can make that attack harder, though the memo does not describe a complete defense against denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: Predictable path selection can help an attacker overload one path. Less predictable hashing can make that attack harder.
